newsitem.title: USA: NYC mayor confident NYS will okay tax bill, agency.
newsitem.headline: NYC mayor confident NYS will okay tax bill, agency.

text.p: New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani on Wednesday predicted that the New York State legislature, which failed to approve key tax and funding bills for the city at a special session, would do so in January.

"We came very close. A great deal of progress was made in coming to an agreement with the Assembly and the Senate on the infrastructure authority and the personal income tax (surcharge) so that if they should come back into session this year or when the come back in January, I am quite confident we'll be able to reach an agreement," Giuliani said.

The legislature's failure to approve the new measures was a major blow to the city, which has projected that it will collect $455 million from the personal income tax, which expires at year-end, in fiscal 1997. City sources, who declined to be named, said the tax still would be collected and then enacted retroactively.

New York City is expected to hit its constitutional debt limit before the fiscal 1997 year ends on June 30, and the city wanted the new bonding agency to sidestep this cap. Giuliani said "minor differences" remained between the Assembly and the city over the new authority.

The breakdown in New York City's talks with the Assembly was blamed in part the city's linking of the tax and agency bills, as the city argued the house should not require it to spend $550 million over two years on schools when it was so close to hitting its debt limit. The Senate's insistence on ending the special session on Tuesday, the same day it began, was another obstacle, they said, suggesting it was unlikely this house would agree to return before January.
Bob Kurtter of Moody's Investors Service said ample time remains for tax levy to be extended and the new agency approved. "They still have time, it's not a crisis yet."
